speechtext: LEWIS (West Huron) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 45) respecting a load line on ships sailing on the inland waters of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Explain.

This Bill has reference to an official load-line on ships sailing on the inland waters of Canada, and also to coasting vessels, but not including foreign ships. It is modelled after the sections of the English Act with reference to the load-line on ships. The purpose of the Bill is to lessen the liability to these very regrettable accidents which happen in the fall of the year, and which cause very great loss of life, as in the case of the 'Jones' two years ago, and the ' Asia ' some years previously. The clause referring to the inland waters applies only after the 15th of September, and until the 15th of May in each year. There is also a clause with reference to the loadline of barges on the coasting waters of Canada, and that clause is modelled on a Bill brought in by Mr. Lawrence, formerly member for Colchester, but which was not passed into law. There is also a clause which obliges the captain who enters his ship outward from each port in Canada after the 15th day of September until the 15th day of May in each year to leave with the customs officers before he gets his clearance a list of every person leaving port on his ship, with names and addresses. There is also a clause with reference to the loading of ships. One of the chief causes of these accidents is that ships are loaded on deck in a hurry to get produce out in the rush in the fall of the year.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

While on this matter, I wish to refer to comment made in at least, one Liberal journal, the Montreal ' Herald.' Notwithstanding my explanation made twice in this House, it repeated the statement a few days ago that I had known immediately after the publication, on the 26th day of October, that the telegram had been altered. I make that announcement for the third time in this House; but I do not doubt that the misrepresentation will continue in certain quarters.

Mr. ANDREW BRODER (Dundas) moved for:
Copy of all correspondence, orders in council, papers and other documents between the government or any member thereof, and any person or persons, referring in any way to the drainage of the Nation river running through the townships of Matilda and Winchester, in the county of Dundas.
He said:-The Nation river has had quite a history with regard to this matter of drainage. That history goes so far back as a considerable time before confederation, when there was a report made on the practicability of bringing the waters from the St. Lawrence river to the Nation river for power purposes. I do not wish to go so far back as that in asking for this correspondence, but I wish to state that previous to the defeat of the Conservative government in 1896, there was an arrangement come to between the people and the government, that if the people would put a dredge in the river the government would work the dredge. That arrangement was carried out for one or two seasons if I remember correctly. The Conservatives were defeated in 1896, and the incoming government carried out the understanding during the balance of that season and part of the following season. The Hon. Mr. Tarte was then Minister of Public Works, and he held the view that the Dominion government had no right to do this work, but he realized the responsibility for carrying out the contract entered into by the previous government, and he went so far as to offer the people a bulk sum as a quittance of the obligation of the government. I am not sure as to the amount mentioned by the Hon. Mr. Tarte of that time, but at all events it was not satisfactory to those who were dredging the river. In answer to the argument that the Dominion government has no right to undertake such work, I might say that the necessity now for draining the river is greater than it was at any time before, because as the country is being cleared the water get3 so rapidly into the river that it overflows its banks and destroys the crops. This takes the question beyond the local standpoint. It has got to be a very serious matter for the people. I may say that the present government have seen fit, for local drainage purposes, to deal with rivers of a similar nature. They have in the county of Prescott, dealing virtually with the same river, laid out quite a large amount of

money at a place called Pitchoff. On the Chateauguay river, in the province of Quebec, in the county of Chateauguay, in the vicinity of St. Chrysostom, the government have laid out, purely for drainage purposes, some $12,000 or $15,000 ; and I think there is an obligation resting on the government to carry out the contract between the previous government and the people with reference to the Nation river. There is no question as to that, because the dredge is there which was built by the people assisted by the Ontario government at that time, as a proof of the contract. The Ontario government assisted by giving $4,000 towards the cost of the dredge. There is no question as to the understanding that was arrived at. The people have expended between $70,000 and $80,000 on that river. The engineers at that time considered that, if the river were enlarged, that would to a very considerable extent relieve the people of the difficulty; but the conditions have so changed that the relief is a very nominal thing to-day. I simply bring the matter to the attention of the government in the hope that they will deal with it on its merits and in accordance with the obligations resting on the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
My hon. friend and myself, from force of circumstances, perhaps know more about the situation of this river than most of the other members of the House. This is a matter which has been before the public, and in which the public in that part of the country have been particularly interested, for, I suppose, twenty-five or thirty years. I had the honour of being a member of the counties' council of the united counties of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry when seme of the practical work in connection with it was undertaken, and I realize what my hon. friend says about the interest taken in that part of the country in the matter. The more the country has been opened up and drained into the Nation river, the more need there has been to get the water away. It is a comparatively small stream at low water, but it contains ledges which high water cause rapids, and the object of the work done has been to remove these ledges and so improve the flow of the water. At certain times the Nation becomes a violent stream, with the water so high that at some places it forms a lake a mile wide, flooding the land in the vicinity, so that sometimes the people are obliged to transfer mails and passengers across the lake by boats. The harm done by the flooding of this river is very great. A great deal of work has been done on it, and just what ought to be done now is a question for consideration. The provincial government has granted some Mr. BRODER.	[DOT]
aid, the Dominion government has also
granted aid in days gone by, and the people have taxed themselves very heavily. It is a matter not purely local, as it is quite wide in its scope. I support the resolution for bringing down the papers in order that the House may see in just what position the matter is.

(Translation.) What is the nature of the work done by the Abbe O'Leary, former professor of history?

(Translation.) He does not work in Paris but in Canada, and he is busy making researches for collecting the historical documents scattered pretty near all over the province of Quebec, and having some bearing on our history. The work he does is under the supervision of Dr. Doughty, in order that we may be able to locate those historical documents.

(L'Islet.) (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, allow me to make a few remarks about our archives. It is with pleasure that I grant the amount of $28,000 here asked for by the Minister of Agriculture to keep up the work of our archives. The literate people stand in with the hon. Minister of Agriculture and encourage him in his patriotic and historical work. We are proud of the record of our country and we must make ourselves familiar with it. What has been done so far stimulates the writers on our history.
By order in council dated April 17, 1907, the Minister of Agriculture has instituted a commission on historical documents. He was most fortunate in his selection of such men as the reverend Abbe Gosselin and Mr. Edmond Roy for the pursuance of such work in our province. It is important that an intelligent classification of our written records should be made in order that they
may be more easily got at by those desirous of studying them. I am pleased to quote among the students in that branch of our archives the reverend Abbe O'Leary, my old professor in history at the Seminary of Quebec. In the last fifty years, Mr. G. B. Faribault, the Abbe Tanguay, the Abbe Verreault and Mr. Joseph Marmette have been in Paris to make researches in the archives there and made very precious discoveries in the way of documents of the highest importance. Those who are working in the French archives under the direction of the Minister of Agriculture are performing a national work.
According to the report of the Minister of Agriculture, students in our history are also getting useful information in the archives in London. The last documents which have been added to the national collection give valuable knowledge on the maritime provinces. Let us keep up these historical searches. Let us be proud of our archives, they are the depository of our national traditions.

(Translation.) I am happy to hear the observations which the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Paquet) has just made. I feel proud over them and I want to thank him most heartily for the good words he spoke in favour of the work performed for our archives. He was quite right in saying that it is necessary that our Canadian records should be preserved. I am pleased to be able to tell him that we have lately erected in Ottawa a fireproof building, a most suitable building, in fact a fine building where they are now deposited. Considerable work was performed in the Bibliotlifeque Nationale of Paris in searching for and sorting documents relating to Canadian history. Messrs. Marmette, Richard and others have gathered such an amount of them that we have been so far unable to have them all copied over, but that part of the work is just now being pressed with all possible celerity.
We have engaged the services of Mr. Big-gar, well known in Canada for his historical researches and studies. This gentleman is now engaged in pursuing this work in Europe, that is in Paris and London. He understands French as well as English. His researches are not confined to Paris alone, but are spread over Spain, Italy and Britain. He is superintending that part of the work in Paris. I should like very much to further press the copying over of those records, but it is not in our power to do so. It is somewhat difficult to get competent men to do this work. In England, we have clerks who are performing this task, and we are carrying on the work of transcription as fast as we possibly can. When I took up my department, Canada was providing $6,000 a year for the archives, but

having found out that there was much more to do in that direction, I am pleased to say that parliament has always voted the increased appropriations which I asked from time to time for the archives. I may say at the same time that those increases were always voted without hesitation not only by the party in power but by the opposition as well. I hope that I shall have in the future the same encouragement that was shown me in the past for the work of the archives. I also hope that under the supervision of Dr. Doughty, a very competent and devoted official, I might say a most enthusiastic official in the pursuance of his duties, all this work will be pressed forward with vigour and to still more satisfactory results.

MONK (Jacques-Cartier.) (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I want to say that we are very much satisfied indeed of the declarations which have just been made by the hon. minister in answer to the remarks offered by my hon. friend from L'Islet (Mr. Paquet). My hon. friend from L'Islet has stated a point to which great importance is added in the province of Quebec, and I believe no other province in the Dominion is as anxious as ours**that the national records should be carefully looked after and properly stored. All of us, my hon. friend from L'lslet, the hon. minister and myself have those records at heart. I am glad the hon. minister has seen fit to do justice to the opposition in acknowledging that we never refused to grant him the sums required for the proper keeping of our records. This seems to surprise him somewhat, but experience must have taught him of old that when the government wants money for legitimate purposes and for the benefit of the public, the opposition never refused its sanction.
We have in Mr. Doughty a gentleman of such consummate competency it would be almost impossible to get a better on than he, and I think we should carry out all the suggestions which might come from him.
Now to come down to practical business, I would like the minister to tell us how he intends spending the $28,000 here asked for. I see that $60,000 were spent in the fiscal year 1908-09. This item is reduced to $28,000 this year. It is not customary for us to complain of any diminution, especially in the present condition of affairs. I believe, on the contrary, that we may congratulate the government for the excursions it may attempt in the field of economy. But we are interested in knowing how such retrenchments are arrived at as compared with the sums expended last year. What does the department intend spending for the archives in France? What staff do we employ just now for the gathering of records ? I know Mr. Biggar by reputation ; I believe he deserves all the good that is said of him. Is he alone engaged in col-Mr. FISHER.
lecting archives in France? I heard the minister say awhile ago that it was hard to get clerical help in France. Are the copies which we intend obtaining for our archives to be made in the national libraries or from documents held by private families whose records are connected with the history of our country ? I believe we can gather at a very low cost in French, all the documents we require, provided we take the necessary precautions.
I would be thankful to the minister for telling us how he will proceed in the course of the coming year to collect copies of those immense books of records which are actually held in France? What proportion of the money which we vote annually will be devoted to this task in the coming year ? There is no doubt that we can secure large returns in employing for that work nobody but absolutely competent men. It is pretty much the same as this in immigration work, but not as much as in the archives. It is possible to employ in immigration work a whole lot of people as was done in the past, to recruit settlers and spend large sums of money worthlessly. I think the hon. minister ought to tell us what he purposes doing with this $28,000 both in France and England in the course of the coming year.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, nobody else but Mr. Biggar worked at the collection of those records in France. We already have a large number of documents selected and laid by in the Bibliotheque Nation-ale, in Paris. We want to have them copied before selecting more, not because it wouldn't be worth our while to press further our researches in that direction, but because we have sufficient records already awaiting transcription. In the meanwhile, Mr. Biggar keeps up his researches in different parts of France, in the private libraries of historical mansions and elsewhere from which he obtained lists of documents that are probably of some interest to Canada. Mr. Biggar takes these matters upon himself and when he comes across documents which bear upon our history, he has the power to have them copied, inasmuch as we cannot get them in Canada. I do not see that I can give more information upon the work that is being carried out in France.

(Translation.) Do the same remarks of the hon. gentleman apply to the work carried on in England? Did Mr. Biggar first made a selection of the documents that are to be copied in England? Do we employ clerical help there in doing the transcription?
(Translation.) It is the same in England as in France.

(Translation.) Now, is the whole of these $28,000 to be affected to this work?

Mr. FI$HER. (Translation.) Oh, no.
(Translation.) How then is this item applied?

(Translation.) Besides Mr. Biggar's salary, $7,000 is provided for researches conducted in Europe under Mr. Biggar's care, then there is the messenger's salary, and certain office work at the archives here, $2,000 There is the salaries of the employees outside of Ottawa and who do not belong to the Civil Service, $2,000. Transcription to be made in Canada, $4,000. Purchase of books, newspapers, &c., $3,500. Printing, $5,000. Expenses by the commission on messengers, $500. And $1,000 for sundry expenses.
(Translation.) The amount of $4,000 for transcription in Canada seems to me pretty high. What documents are there to copy? Are they documents belonging to private collections?

(Translation.) Most of those historical documents, if not all, are held in the court houses at Montreal, Quebec and Three Rivers. Quite a number of them are also to be found at the provotship in Quebec. Others are to be found elsewhere. This sum provides for the transcription of these documents.

(Translation.) I do not want to keep up unduly the discussion upon an item which is not opposed, but it seems to me that the sum which we affect to transcription of documents held in Canada, is higher than should be in relation to the results obtained. It might be that the returns are commensurate to the amount of money spent, but I doubt it. I believe that for a young nation like us, whose records are so extensive and which desires to extend the lasting work of its national history, we appropriate a sum of money rather inadequate to the task.
In reviewing the budget, I could easily find a great number of items which are extremely high and which are devoted to purposes less interesting, less urgent than the keeping of our archives. On this subject I may say that we, on the opposition side, will ever be ready to grant all items asked by the government, even if the amount was higher than this one, provided that it would be clearly stated what use it is intended for. If they are deserving and free of all waste, if practically, they would increase the volume of our national archives, they will receive our cordial support.
There is presently, in England and in France as in Canada, number of papers which are in danger of being lossed, and it is necessary that we should have in the administration of this department-which is much more important than we believe-men in every way able to keep them. We will always be willing to vote the moneys necessary for this object. I must say before resuming, that the hon. minister has made since a few years most commendable efforts, for the preserving of our archives.
I see that Professor Adam Shortt received $1,675. He received $1,500 for editing constitutional documents. Is Professor Shortt employed by the year to do that or was it simply a contract?

Professor Shortt was not employed by the year. This is work of an exceptional character, requiring a man of exceptional attainments. There was no question about Professor Shortt's qualifications for the work, and an arrangement was made with him that he should do it and we should pay him accordingly.
In what way?
He sent in an account which on careful examination was considered to be fair and just and reasonable, and we paid it.
Was it by the day or just a lump sum?
Just a lump sum. He did this at odd times during almost three years.
I see that during the same time Professor Shortt received $2,500 from the Labour Department for acting in connection with labour disputes.
I think all of this work was performed before he acted in the labour disputes.
What is the salary paid to the archivist?
$3,200 a year.
Has he an assistant?
No, he has no assistant archivist. Mr. Edmor Roy is the next official in the archives branch, but he has not been called assistant archivist.

It seems to me that Mr. Doughty's position and qualifications are sufficiently important to place him upon the same footing as the deputy head of a department. His work requires very important qualifications and Dr. Doughty possesses them in an eminent degree. He has no assistant and is called upon to bring into life a new department. I think the House would be quite ready to vote him a larger salary than that.

I am very glad to hear my hon. friend say that. Dr. Doughty is now in the Civil Service and is subject of course to the Civil Service rules, like the heads of other branches. I do not think a department ought to be created unless there is a considerable amount of administration and detail work which there is not in that case.

I did not advocate making a department; I submitted that the duties

are sufficiently important and require high enough qualifications to justify Dr. Doughty being placed on about the same footing as the deputy head of a department.
I asked the minister about the $32,000 reduction in salaries?
In the first place I am informed that Mr. Roy's salary of $3,000 was not included in the Auditor General's Report. He was appointed since it was prepared, in March of last year.
Is the whole Archives branch now subject to the new Civil Service Act?
Yes.
So that in future persons who are employed in that department will be recommended by the Civil Service Commissioners?
Yes.

I am very glad of that, and I join in what my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has said with regard to Dr. Doughty's qualifications, which in my opinion are of a very eminent order; I feel that the country would be placed in a very unfortunate position if we should lose his services. As far as I am concerned I would be very glad indeed to support the government in placing his salary upon a better basis than it is at present, because I know how extremely assiduous he has been in the work in which he is engaged. It is more than a mere matter of duty with him, it is not only a duty but a pleasure, the work of his life, and from personal observation of the work which he is performing, I have formed a very high appreciation of the services he has rendered the country since he has been placed at the head of the Archives department.

I do not think that anyone in or out of the government appreciates or understands Dr. Doughty's work more than I do. I take a good deal of credit to myself for having got Dr. Doughty to become the Archivist, and I understand and fully appreciate not only the quality of his work but his personal character and devotion to that work which is of a very peculiar character, and which there are not many men qualified to perform. I know of no one in Canada as well qualified as Dr. Doughty.
The minister has not yet explained the $32,000.

The Auditor General's Report does not show the salary of Mr. Roy of $3,000 and another of $1,000 or $1,200. That is in addition to the $28,000 of salaries which are transferred from payments from the Archives branch to the civil government. Dr. Doughty made out an estimate of what he required this year and the esti-Mr. MONK.	,
mate came to less than $28,000. He asked for that $28,000 to carry on work outside of the work provided for by the salaries. $28,000 has been transferred to civil government and there is $28,000 of work to be done outside of this out of the vote to Archives.
Patent Record, $17,000.
That is paid almost entirely to the King's Printer ?

Altogether.
Census and statistics, $11,500.
There is a decrease.

There is a transfer of $28,850 of salaries to civil government, but I have asked for $5,000 more for other work of the census and statistics branch. If it had not been for asking for that $5,000 more the vote would have been reduced by $6,500. I have asked for $5,000 additional to be applied to the work of issuing monthly crop bulletins, which we undertook last summer, and hope to continue.
That will be spent for salaries?
No, that is outside work. None of this vote will be spent for salaries in Ottawa, but it will be required for printing, correspondence and the expense of getting out these crop statistics.
What is the total cost of the Census Department each year?
The total cost for the coming year will be $28,450 in salaries under civil government, and $11,500, which brings the total to $40,000 in round figures.
Will that be an increase over last year?
An increase of $5,000.
How many civil servants are engaged in the department?
Twenty-nine in Ottawa.
Has there been a material increase in the last few years?

No, not material. Of course in the census years there were many more, but since the compilation and completion of the last decennial census they have not been increased practically at all. I will not say there has not been one or two added at some time or other, but practically there has been no increase.
I would like to ask the minister to explain the system adopted in collecting these -crop statistics.

The system has been practically this: We have tried to find farmers throughout the country, who have shown by some correspondence or connection with the department with other work, that

they are men of intelligence and take an interest in the agricultural work of their particular sections. These have been communicated with and asked to send in perio-u rePor^s' which they do by mail, and are ^en made up into the estimates which these bulletins contain. We do not pay these correspondents anything. We expect them to do it, and we, in return, give them the advantage of sending bulletins to them and any other information from the department which they wish to have.
Is not that a duplication of the work carried on by the various provincial governments?

Some of the provincial governments do that kind of work, but there is no such work done generally for the whole of Canada. We do make use of the bulletins and reports that the provinces issue for the purpose of checking these statistics, but that work, being done only by some provinces, does not give the results for the whole Dominion which we require to have.
Are these bulletins issued weekly or monthly?
Monthly.

May I ask the minister if it is not possible for him to gather together a greater volume of statistics in regard to the trade of foreign countries? During the past few years we have been urging upon the minister the necessity of enlarging the statistics in that regard and giving us seme comparisons between Canada and other countries similarly situated, the Argentine Republic, for instance, or some other foreign countries. I know it would require some research, but I cannot help feeling that we are not in touch with the statistics regarding the trade and commerce of these countries to the extent that we should be. I know that the department have improved somewhat in that regard in the last few years, but I would like to urge upon the minister the necessity of making further investigation and trying to bring down a more complete statement with regard to the trade and commerce of different countries, especially with regard to the exports and imports of products such as we produce from our own farms, mines and timber areas.

I can understand the value of such information and the convenience of having it. But, we would simply have to go to the same documents that are now available to any individual. We might, of course, compile them and work them up into different forms of comparative tables. But I may say to my hon. friend quite frankly, that we have so much more to do in regard to our own statistics than we have been able to do, that I have hesitated
to turn the labours of my own staff, or the money which is voted by parliament for this purpose, to the compilation of statistics outside of Canada. I have in my mind much that we might do in Canada in the way of getting statistics which we have not yet done and which I would like to see done and that is one reason why, in this work, I am asking for $5,000 more than I did last year. It is to try and increase the amount of information to be given out and made available for our own people about our own work. I think it would be better to spend the money and devote our time and energies to our own work than to foreign work which is done in each country for itself and the results of which are largely available in the library for those who wish to study them.

I quite agree with the minister in regard to this information being available in the library and that is why I cannot understand why it would not be comparatively easy to gather these statistics together. If they can be gathered without a great deal of effort out of books in the library, the people in Canada who are desirous of getting in touch with these statistics not being able to come to Ottawa and investigate for themselves, would be put in possession of this information. It would be a source of interest to our people in general to have this information to a greater extent than they have at the present time.

I would like to ascertain from the minister whether or not the annual statistics compiled with respect to some of our own matters should not be made a little more complete and should not be made to conform more to the information that is set forth in the decennial census returns. I have not made any careful examination of the yearly statistics that are produced in the Census Department as compared with the results of the decennial census of 1901 except in one respect, and that was to endeavour to obtain from the last statistical report respecting lumber such information as would enable me to ascertain whether or not the lumber cut in various particulars had increased and to what extent, since 1901. I found that they did not seem to run on the same lines. There was not the same division of production. Could not that be accomplished? For example, in the census of 1901 there are returns for so much sawn lumber, so many cubic feet of timber, so many cords of wood for fuel, so many railway ties, but when we come to ' Census and Statistics Bulletin No. 2, issued at Ottawa, 1907,' I do not get information of the same character as is contained in the census with reference to the lumber industry, and it is, therefore, impossible to make a comparison.
1 may add that upon application to the officers of the Census Department I received every possible assistance and all the in-

formation they had in their possession, and what I say is not by way of censuring them in any way, but for the purpose of ascertaining whether a better method cannot be devised. Possibly this particular information may appertain more properly to the Forestry Branch of the Department of the Interior when that is placed in good working order. From the yearly reports of the United States you can ascertain practically all the information about the production of lumber that you would obtain in the decennial census. In the Forestry Eeport of the United States for 1906 it is stated that they had obtained returns from about 12,000 mills in the United States with regard to sawn lumber. If the information published in our bulletins could be systematized a little better it would be much more valuable.

I am informed that there is about the same difference between the information in the American decennial census and their yearly reports as there is in our publications. The blue book which the hon. gentleman refers to gives the return of manufactured lumber and not what might, be called crude lumber cut in the forest. I quite agree that it is best to make the figures as nearly similar in character as possible in all our publications so as to enable comparison. I will discuss the matter with the chief statistician.

This bulletin gives the number of establishments, the capital, the number of employees, the wages for labour,, and the value of the product, but it does not give the quantity of the product. I know that you can obtain from the forestry service of the United States all the information respecting the annual production that you get in their decennial census.
I am very glad to have suggestions of that kind because they will all help to perfect the various bulletins which we issue.

I have in my hand a bulletin entitled ' Census and Statistics, Monthly, No. 7, Vol. 2, January, 1907, published by authority of the Minister of Agriculture,' and I suppose this report is issued by Mr. Archibald Blue. I think sufficient care is not taken in the preparation of statistics with a view of their absolute correctness so as to make them of practical value. For instance, in this bulletin I find it stated that the average wage for farm help in Canada is $24.60 per month for males and $13.50 for females, but it is not stated whether that wage includes board and lodging. Perhaps the minister can say what the intention was.
The statement ought to have been made in that table that those wages were in addition to board and lodging in these cases.
That certainly should be stated.
I agree with you.

The idea conveyed by the bulletin is that the wages are paid to that extent during the whole twelve months of the year, whereas they are not paid for more than six or eight months. That is misleading to people wishing to come to this country.

I cannot offhand answer the question; I shall have to look into the matter and see. Of course, wages do vary at different seasons of the year; but I took it that when they were put down in the bulletin as being so much a month, that meant the average of the year.

The wages as given in this bulletin are both the monthly and the yearly wages for males for the whole of Canada, namely, $24.60 a month or by the year $209, which would practically be $17.50 a month. I apprehend that $24.60 would only apply to certain months of the year. The danger of this report is that no doubt some copies of it will go to the old country and people coming to this country and relying upon it will be surprised. If, as the minister says, the board and lodging are included, I think it is unfair to Canada to place in the hands of the people in the old country statements that do not convey the full information they might reasonably expect. I think the hon. member for Dufferin is correct, that the wages per month applies only to say six months of the year.

The figures which purport to give the rates of wages for farm hands and female servants, leaving out of consideration board and lodging, are very misleading. It is well known that all over the country farm hands and domestic servants get their board and lodging, and these are always taken into consideration in fixing wages. In the future compilation of these figures, I think it would be well to give the wages for six months in summer and the wages for six months in winter. This would convey a more accurate idea to the general public and those interested, and the fact that board and lodging are taken into consideration should be distinctly stated in publications bearing the stamp of the Minister of Agriculture.

In the Auditor General's Report, page E 9, I find this item: ' Amounts paid secretary treasurers of municipalities for lists of farmers, $1,074.74.' Did the minister send for lists to the secretary treasurers of all the municipalities, or were some favoured above others ?

I am informed that when the lists of farmers were being made up, the

secretary treasurers of municipalities were in many cases asked to supply lists. That was done only in Quebec and the maritime provinces, as we had the information for the other provinces.
How did you obtain that information for the other provinces ?
We got it from the provincial governments.
Why could you not utilize the voters' lists in the different municipalities ?
The voters' lists do not show who are farmers.
Why could you not get the lists for Quebec and the maritime provinces as well as Ontario ?
The provincial governments in those provinces had no lists.
What would be the nature of the prosecutions in regard to the census ?

I think they were for the refusal by some persons to give the information required by the Census Act.
Statistical Year Book, $6,000.

The subject of our Statistical Year-book is one which has been discussed every year for many years past. Ours is the most miserable Year-book published by any country, bar none. It is a wretched Year-book. Perhaps my hon. friend the minister will remember that several years ago we had a very long discussion in this House, in which the subject was threshed out completely. A member from Nova Scotia, Mr. Ross, who is now in the Senate, brought in all the year-books published by all the great British dependencies, and compared them, in regard to the printing, the forms, the manner in which they were prepared, with our own. In the year-books prepared in Australia and New Zealand, the information is carefully classified, and is given in a very pleasing form, which attracts the eye of the strang-eri Our Year-book lacks all these elements It is as dry as the Public Accounts Blue-book
There is nothing grouped in it in such a manner as to attract attention. That is a defect which we ought to remove. $5,000 or $6,000 additional is nothing. We spend immense sums to attract immigrants. We make folders, we encourage newspapers, political friends of the government, to the tune of from $50,000 to $100,000 to publish absurd, useless information and we do not seem to be able, although this matter has been frequently discussed and criticised and protested against, to produce a good Yearbook. Here is another point. Our Yearbook is published very) late. The one last
published is that of 1907. We ought to have our Year-book of the last year published at the very beginning of the new year, and surely it is possible to have a staff sufficient and competent to collect all the information and have it published at, the beginning of the year. Compare our Year-book with that of New Zealand. The latter has maps of the different parts of that country and photographs, and is a book which you could send to any one who desires information about that country. You cannot publish a proper book for $6,000-such a book as could be circulated in our schools and abroad. It is about time we made a new start in this matter, it is essential that a young growing country like ours, about which information is sought on all sides and by all classes of people, should publish a complete and interesting information on our possibilities and resources. Other countries take a pride in publishing Year-books infinitely superior to ours. What we are publishing is simply a waste of money.

If we go back four or five years, we find that the Year-book now published is not equal to what was then published. We then had the returns of other countries and a lot of other valuable information not given in the present publication. We either should publish a Year-book which we will not be ashamed to send out to those desiring information or not publish one at all. Would the Minister of Agriculture inform us how many were published in 1907 and when we may expect to get the Year-book of 1908?

I am not at all convinced by my hon. friends of the advisability of doing what they suggest. Years ago our Year-book was increasing in bulk to such an extent as to contain a good deal of duplication of tables and a great deal of information about foreign countries not at all necessary for our purposes. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) say3 rightly that New Zealand published a very attractive pictorial volume, very much of the nature of a picture book, but I do not think that is what we ought to expect in a statistical year-book. And I know that the Commonwealth of Australia to-day has discarded that type of work and is now issuing a book of the same character as our own. The Year-books of European governments are of the same character as ours. They do not go into long descriptive accounts of the country, and voluminous dissertations on its industries. Such things are out of place in a statistical year-book. Such a book ought only to contain statistical information compiled so as to be available to the student who wants accurate information of that kind. That I think, we have accomplished. I do not think that the Canadian Year-book ought to be expected to contain information about other countries. That

information can be found in the Year-books of these countries.

Every one has not the opportunity of having access to the Yearbook of other countries. A good deal of the information contained in former Year-books, which has been left out of the present edition, was of great) convenience to students and others.
If I were to adopt that suggestion. I would have to load down our Year-book to such an extent that it would be a volume no one would want to handle.
That was not the case in the past.
Our Year-book in 1896-1897 was a very bulky volume.
A great deal better that the present one.

I do not think so for the purpose for which it is printed. It may have had reading matter for people who want this class of reading, but it was not a useful and complete volume of statistical tables concerning our own country. I am sorry if hon. gentlemen do not agree with me in that. But my judgment in the matter was formed after a good deal of hesitation. And I find my opinion in accord with the practice of older countries in Europe and of the United States as well, for they issue year-books of the same character as ours. And, while Australia in days gone by, did as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has explained, it has come round to our view, and to-day the latest Yearbook from Australia is compiled and printed exactly on the line of our own. New Zealand, I think, issues such a year-book as was formerly issued, but I think I am safe in saying that it is the only country that does so. This seems to be confirmation of our judgment and practice in making our Year-book what it is.

(Translation.) May I request that the Minister will make every possible effort to let us have as soon as possible the French edition of the Year Book. I will take advantage of the opportunity to request that he will also hasten the publication of the French copy of the report on Co-operative Associations.

(Translation.) The last mentioned volume is under the control of the Minister of Labour. I shall, however, take care that the request of the hon. member for L'Islet is duly transmitted to him.
As for the Canadian Statistical Year Book, I may say that I have endeavoured to have the English and French copies sent to the Printing Bureau on the same day. In my Department I have issued instructions that all bulletins and reports are to Mr. FISHER.
be translated without delay and the English and French copies forwarded to the printer at the same time. It was found impossible to do this immediately, but I will endeavour to have the order carried out in the future.

I asked my hon. friend (Mr. Fisher) a question which, I think, he has not answered. How is it that our Yearbook comes out so late ? The last Yearbook out, I think, is the one of 1907. That is a year behind. Why cannot we have the Year-book at the beginning of the year, giving the results of the year just closed? If the minister holds that the Year-book should only give statistics alone, with nothing to please the eye, no maps, nothing which we saw in the Year-books from other countries displayed on the table, why should it take a year to produce it? Why cannot we have it as promptly as other statistical compilations?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) knows that the Year-book is compiled from the reports of the different departments and statistical reports. It takes a little time to compile the figures after these reports are out.

Some time ago 1 received a letter from one of my constituents asking me to ascertain the quantity of mica produced in Canada and the quantity exported. I sent the letter to the Department of Customs and received an answer from the commissioner giving me the quantity exported, but explaining that he could not give me the information as to the quantity produced in the country. I had a copy of the Year-book lying on my desk, and, opening it, I saw the heading:^ ' Mineral products by quantity and value.' So I sent my corespondent the Year-book. Meeting him on the street the other day I asked him if he had received it, and he said that he had, but that it gave him no information. He said it showed the quantity produced in 1901. But what is the use of publishing in 1908 the figures for 1901? Any other information that it had he had already received in the Trade and Commerce and other returns. If we are to have a Year-book, and if we are to have a bureau and a staff charged with the duty of compiling information for the use of the public, what is the good of republishing information from the census of 1901? We ought to have in the department information as to the products of mines right up to date and not only information eight years old. The gentleman who asked the information of me is a manufacturer in Gananoque, but he found that the Year-book gave him nothing but information which he already had.

I speak subject to correction, but I think that if the gentleman had looked over other pages of the book he would have found information from the

Mines branch giving later information. The last authentic returns are those of the census of 1901, and they are put into the Yearbook for that reason. But the Mines branch makes estimates and has returns every year, and I think I am right in saying that my hon. friend would have found compilation of these figures in the Year-book as well as that which he did find.
Would not the reports of the Mines Departments of the various provincial governments give the information pretty well up to date?

I had the pleasure of presenting the recently published Year-book to the representative of a large financial institution in London, and, after looking it over for a time, he said that in the course of his business he became somewhat familiar with the Year-books of many countries, and the Canadian Year-book furnished the greatest information in the shortest and most convenient shape of any that he had seen.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Civil Service Commission, salaries, $30,575.

These estimates were before the House on a former occasion, and at the request of the Prime Minister were allowed to stand in order that certain corrections might be made. The salary of the secretary appears in the estimates as $3,050; this should be $2,900.
In addition to admitting candidates to the Civil Service, does the Civil Service Commission control promotions in the different departments ?

There is a difference between appointment and promotion. The deputy head of a department recommends the promotion and the commission must grant their certificate approving of the promotion before it can be made.
The commission must accept the deputy's recommendation ?
No, they are not bound to accept it.
They examine the candidate before granting the certificate.
I do not think they are bound to examine.
Has the commission anything to do with the outside service ?
No.

Have the Civil Service Commissioners laid before the government a 23
general scheme setting forth the method of holding the examinations and their scheme of procedure ?

The commissioners are preparing a set of regulations to be laid before the government which I understand will form part of the report to be laid before the House. The commissioners have been in conference with the heads of several leading universities and other institutions for the purpose of securing a uniform standard for examinations throughput the country. They have not yet absolutely decided on that standard and for that reason the regulations have not been laid before the government. They have held examinations along lines laid down by themselves and from the candidates successful at these examinations they have recommended several candidates for the Civil Service.
I suppose we will have these regulations before the estimates are all passed ?
If they are submitted to the government in time they will be laid before the House. They will be given to the House at the earliest possible date.
Will the commission recognize the certificates of those who passed before the introduction of the new Civil Service Act as a qualification ?
Yes. The commission have recently notified persons who have passed the examinations in times past to send in their names, addresses and dates of passing so that they will have a list ready.
Will successful candidates be qualified without further examination ?	[DOT]
I cannot answer that.
Have the places at which examinations will be held been announced?
That is a matter within the discretion of the commissioners; they may select different places in the Dominion to suit the convenience of the public.
There seems to be an unusually large staff. The commission did not get under way, did it?
They are just getting under way.
Are they to be located in Ottawa?
The headquarters are to be in Ottawa.

I do not like to press my hott. friend unduly, but I think the committee will admit that it would be more satis-



factory in voting these amounts for this new arrangement that is going into effect this year to have before us the regulations and plan upon which these commissioners intend to proceed. But we will take the assurance of my hon. friend on that point that we shall get them.
Yes.

Therefore, we are passing this vote of $19,000 pretty much on the assumption that everything will be all right. I will call my hon. friend's attention, however, to this: There are two commissioners at $5,000 and a secretary at $3,050.

I was going to observe that it seemed a little high, but we will leave that. Then, there is one examiner at $900, one at $600, and one, Mr. DeCelles, at $600. These, I understand, will assist the commissioners to superintend the competition for entry into the Civil Service. But, I do not understand this: In subdivision B we have three other examiners at $800.
They are clerks employed in the office.
I understood these were examiners, and I was wondering why we wanted examiners in the different subdivisions.

They are not examiners; they do clerical work in the office of the commissioners in Ottawa. I might explain further that there was an error in the item to which my hon. friend has just drawn attention. The proof was corrected and the , item should have been printed in accordance with that correction. That item of $2,100 should have gone into the item below, the. first item under 'contingencies,' and it should have read:
Amount required to pay temporary examiners and to meet the cost of holding the different examinations required by law, $10,000.
These items should not have been separated and the total will be $2,250 less than as it appears here. Then the other items under ' civil government ' relate solely to the Ottawa staff required by the commission.
Who is the secretary of the commission?
Mr. William Foran, formerly secretary of the Board of Civil Service Examiners.
Is it the purpose to examine candidates individually or in a body in a hall?
I understand that examination papers are set and that the competitors write as they do at a University examination.	i
Then why the necessity of three examiners?
Because examinations are held simultaneously at different places, and these examiners are required to conduct them.
Will the same number of examinations be held each year as formerly?

The dates at which the examinations are to be held and the number of examinations are two of the matters before the commission. I do not think they are restricted as to places or dates. My understanding is that they intend to hold examinations more frequently than formerly.
Will the permanent examiners be kept on during the whole year or just at the time the examinations are being held?

Just at the time the examinations are being held. It is not the intention to have any permanent examiners. That item is incorrectly printed. It should have given the total amount for these examinations as $10,000. The wording of the item as it appears here was applicable to the former Board of Civil Service Examiners. There were permanent examiners attached to the board and this is a relic of the former system.
Do I understand the minister to say that it has not yet been decided where the examinations will be held?
The Civil Service Commissioners have not yet decided upon the number of places where examinations will be held.

I would ask the minister to bear in mind that there are a number of people in British Columbia and the west who would like to enter into this competition and some provision should be made to hold examinations in those provinces.

These are the matters that are engaging the attention of the Board and that is the reason why the regulations that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) referred to are not yet complete. It is to meet such contingencies that the regulations are being framed.

How have the appointments been made since the 1st of September? The Act came into force on that date and after that date it was necessary to appoint to the inside service by competitive examination. Have all persons appointed since that date been appointed by competitive examination?
So I understand.
How has that been accomplished?

There were examinations held a couple of months ago, and I do not know of any appointments having been made prior to that. I understand that any appointments that were made were appointments based upon the result of those examinations.
Does the hon. gentleman know whether or not the old examinations have been utilized for that purpose?

I do not know to what extent the results of the former examinations have been utilized, but I am informed that a number of temporary clerks have been brought on for temporary work who had passed the previous examinations. A few moments ago I explained to another hon. gentleman that the Commission had inserted notices in the papers asking those that had previously passed the Civil Service Examination under the old board to send in their names, addresses and the dates upon which they had passed the examination, so that they might have them for reference.
Are there not records of these examinations in the department and in the hands of the present Civil Service Examiners?
There are.

So that I suppose they could have been resorted to for the purpose pending the holding of new examinations? I do not know whether it would be in strict compliance with the statute or not, but in default of anything better it would have been wise to have utilized them.

I have had one experience with reference to the new Act. An officer died in one of our branches and the vacancy had to be filled. In accordance with the wishes of the commissioners, the deputy of the department addressed a communication to them stating that we required another clerk in subdivision B, or whatever it was-I think in the class running from $800 to $1,000. He expressed a wish that they would give him a name of a clerk, stating that he would have to do accounting work and suggesting that he should be good at figures and have a retentive memory. They simply, from the records now before them, I suppose, selected a young man and sent him to us. We do not pass an outside clerk making the appointment. The commissioners decide on the person who is to be appointed, they notifv the Auditor General, and he comes on without any outside clerk being passed. He must have three months' trial. The deputy cannot object to him until he has had three months' trial, then if he finds he cannot do the work, he must within six months notify the commissioners that he is incompetent for the work and they give us another person. But, if
231	. ;i II! Hi :im
the deputy does not notify them within six months that the person they have sent is incompetent he becomes permanent.
Who are the other permanent examiners? I see there is one gentleman named.
These were the old examiners. The other two were Dr. J. C. Glashan, Inspector of Public Schools in Ottawa, and Dr. Thorburn.
Do they act in a body or does each go to a different place and hold an examination?
They go as directed by the Board.
They go individually to hold an examination
Yes.
And the paners are examined by these men and the result sent to the commissioners?
Yes.
Do I understand that the $900 and the $600 respectively are paid to these men for holding an examination half-yearly?

I do not know that it is correct to say that these gentlemen will only hold semi-annual examinations. I understand the examinations are to be held more frequently than formerly and held in different provinces so as to give a larger number a chance to compete. I cannot speak with exactitude at the moment, but I understand these gentlemen do perform other duties than merely attending at the examinations.
They perform other duties besides that?

Yes, and it is not the
intention to have these men permanent as was the case under the old system. They will be selected by the commissioners from time to time, and this vote is to provide funds to pay these gentlemen.
Then am I to understand that no matter how many examinations are held the total salaries will be $600 and $900 respectively?
These were the salaries received by the examiners on the old board.
Did I understand that these examiners were to be sent from one province to another to hold examinations?
I understand that is the intention.
The system formerly was that the examination papers were pre-
It is a pity the minister was not able to give us that explanation.
If these Toermanent examiners are to be sent from place to place, what is the necessity for temporary examiners?

I understand there will he no permanent examiners in the sense that they were permanent under the old system. I shall, with the permission of the House, read the explanation that has been made to me:-
The scheme of competitive examination provided by the Civil Service Act will necessitate the employment of many outside examiners who will be entrusted with the preparation of questions and the marking of the candidates' papers, and the expenditure for this work alone will be considerable, especially as it is proposed to hold the general competitive examinations twice a year.
In addition to this there will be the remuneration to the presiding examiners and their assistants at some eighteen centres throughout the Dominion, as well as the rent to be paid for halls and the necessary furniture to equip them for examination purposes. Then again it is not improbable that a number of special technical examinations will be required during the year, for which the services of outside examiners will be utilized, and which will entail some expense. While the commission can only estimate approximately what the cost will be for the different services during the first year under the new system, it is fully expected that the amount asked for will be required.
It is hoped before the close of the next fiscal year to submit for the approval of the Governor in Council a regular tariff of charges for the different services required under the new Act.

I do not see what difference it makes whether you call them permanent examiners or what you call them. I want to know what these men do for the salaries of $900 and $600, and the distinction between them, and what are called temporary examiners?

There is another thing that I would like the hon. gentleman to explain at the same time, that is, whether or not the scheme is the same as the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, has explained, or the one that he himself has explained, because they are entirely different. The scheme which has hitherto prevailed, as far as I understand the explanation which was given, is that the papers have all been marked by a central body of examiners at Ottawa. The scheme outlined in the memorandum which the Secretary of State has read refers to a system of marking at different places by examiners appointed for those places. That is a very different thing, and we would like to know definitely just how that is going to work out. If you have a system of competitive examinations, how will you work out the scheme of having papers marked by twelve or eighteen different examiners throughout the country ? The system of

marking cannot be precisely the same. Of course, I speak with a great deal of deference, so far as the proposal is concerned, because no doubt the Civil Service Examiners have bestowed a great deal of consideration upon it. That, however, would strike me as an initial difficulty. I do not understand at the present moment how the system will be worked out, and would be glad to have further explanations.
I do not know that the actual marking will be done at the outside places.
If I caught the memorandum correctly, it did say that.

It provides that the outside examiners shall be entrusted with putting the questions and marking the examination papers. Then it goes on to indicate that the presiding examiners may have assistance at these different centres. That is the only information I have on the subject.
I would like to have an answer to my question.

I do not observe that it is the intention of the commission to make any difference between permanent and temporary. As I have already explained, the term permanent examiners is a misprint, and should not have appeared.

Section 11 of the Civil Service Act contains this provision :
The present civil service examiners shall continue to hold office during pleasure and shall be under direction of the commission.
As I understand, under this provision, the three Civil Service Examiners continue in office during pleasure.

Messrs. DeCelles, Thor-burn and Glashan are the three gentlemen who form that board, I do not understand that it is the intention to continue them for any length of time, but it is intended to select such gentlemen as may be available for the purposes of these examinations- not necessarily these three gentlemen.
This item refers to these three gentlemen, does it not ?
Yes.

Up to the present time it has evidently been the pleasure of the government to continue these three men in office. My hon. friends on the treasury benches do not seem to be familiar with their own orders in council, because I find in a return brought down to-day an order in council of the 16th of October, which, after reciting that the Civil Service Commissioners are engaged in formulating a code of rules and regulations for competitive examinations, provides :
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Secretary of State, aoting on the advice of the Civil Service Commissioners, is pleased to order and it is hereby ordered, in order that the interests of the publio service may not suffer, and in order that everything may be done in compliance with the strict requirements of the law, that until such time as the rules and regulations above indicated are established by the Governor in Council, the ordinary entrance examinations or their equivalent, heretofore accepted for the inside service, and still required for the outside service, shall be the test for the employment of clerks in the third division of the inside service as prescribed by the said amending Act; it being nevertheless distinctly understood that, even in this interim arrangement, the competitive system shall prevail in such entrance examinations, that is to say, that those having the highest percentages in passing the entrance examinations in question shall be given the preference in appointments made as above set forth.
That is what I suggested a moment ago might very properly have been done. I am finding no fault with the order in council, but I think we might have had the explanation given a little more fully, so that we [DOT] could have understood what the situation was.
I may say that I was not in office when that order in council was passed.
I was not finding fault with the hon. gentleman any more than the other ministers.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if the examiners just referred to have anything to do with examining applicants for positions in the permanent force; for I see at page 52 of the estimates an item of $700 to pay Civil Service Examiners for examining applicants for commission in the permanent force.
I can give no explanation of that. It must be some arrangement in the Militia Department to employ the old Civil Service Examiners; but it is not under the Civil Service Act.
Is this $700 appropriated for this service included in the salaries of the examiners ?
It must be extra pay.

I fully agree with the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. S. Sharpe) that twelve men appear to be a very large number to examine persons for positions in the Civil Service. I should think that three or four at the outside could accomplish that work. Here is a staff of twelve men which is going to cost the country about $30,000 a year. It is simply an outrage.
They are! the masters- the absolute masters now.
What is the average number of new appointments made each year in the Civil Service.
I cannot give that information.
How many in your own department?
There have not been any that I am aware of.

According to the statements of some of the ministers the other evening, there were in the last year only five or six appointments in each of their departments. If there are, say ten or eleven departments, with an average of five or six appointments during the year in each, that would mean some 60 new appointments and it is going to cost $30,000 per year simply to examine applicants to fill that number of positions. Surely the Secretary of State must have an estimate of how many vacancies there are to fill each year on an average.
I can only answer for my own department, andi there were none in it last year.
I should say, speaking offhand, there are in the neighbourhood of 150 new appointments each year. I am simply making a statement from what 1 know from experience in the last ten years

Will the Secretary of State agree to give us, on some other estimate, a memorandum showing how many vacancies there were in each department during the year 1908, and the number of vacancies and new positions that were filled?
just the same as if there were a hundred positions to be filled.
Are the examinations held in dierent provinces ?
Yes, if one clerk has to be apDointed, opportunity must be given everyone throughout the Dominion to compete.

Perhaps my hon. friend could explain a matter I inquired about some time ago. Is it proposed that there shall be certain papers sent and that the answers of the candidates shall be marked by the examiners in different cities and different parts of the country?

I cannot give an absolute answer. The same examination papers will be used everywhere and will be prepared and sent to wherever the examinations are going to take place just as in the old examinations. I cannot say whether the answers are all sent in to the central body here to pass upon, but I think that will be the case.
I received a contrary impression from the memorandum given by the Secretary of State, and I thought that possibly the Minister of Agriculture would be able to speak definitely upon the subject.

Is it the intention of the commission to apportion the appointments from the different provinces according to population? In the United States the appointments are made to the Civil Service from the different states in proportion to their population.
There is no such provision in the Civil Service Act.
I shall try to get that at the earliest date posible.
Taking the statement of the Minister of Agriculture that there were probably 150 vacancies filled last year, along with the commission he engaged in making the selections.

The commission have a year's work to do before they can get the lists from which to select those people. They have to hold examinations all over the country. They have to prepare the papers and organize the examinations and under the new Act they have to prepare special examinations for technical officers and others. So that they not only have to hold two large examinations once every six months, of the ordinary class of applicant, but also special examinations. I have myself three cases in which I shall have to apply to the commissioners in a very few days for examination for officers, and in each case there will have to be special papers drawn and opportunity will have to be given to every one in Canada to compete, Mr. PATERSON.

I would like a little better explanation in answer to the question I put. You can say that this item is wrong, if you like, but if you take the two items you will find they make a total of $10,000. If this item is wrong, why is one of these men put down at $900 and the other at $600?

This item was in continuance of the practice that prevailed under the old plan of Civil Service examination. The intention is, and should have been carried out, to strike out that item, a lump sum of $10,000 being asked for to hold these examinations here and in the eighteen centres referred to in the memorandum.
But that does not explain why one man is given $900 and one man $600.

One of these men is Dr. Glashan, inspector of schools for Ottawa. Not being a member of the Civil Service, he was given $600. The others are members

of the Civil Service and they were given $600 for one and $900 for the other.
What were his duties?
Their duties were to prepare the papers for examinations, send them out and examine and mark them when they came back.
It cost $2,100 before, and it will cost us $30,000 hereafter.
Besides the examinations, we have the services of the Civil Service Commission.

Is it the intention to have the Civil Service examining body carry on examinations for the various branches of the service? For instance, there is a vote to be proposed of $11,000 for examination of masters and mates. I understand this does not now come under the Civil Service any more than the examinations for the permanent force, but I understand there has been a great deal of abuse in connection with this examination.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. A. Currie) is wandering from the item before us.

I simply ask whether
this central body will carry on these various examinations.
The Civil Service Commissioners, operating under the Act of last session, do not conduct examinations for the outside service.

I do not wish to delay the committee, but it seems to me that we are asked to vote this money pretty much in the dark. Many of the questions which we are compelled to ask would have been unnecessary if somebody had done the preparatory work showing why the money is asked for. We ought to have the regulations prepared by these commissioners. I do not wish to delay the Secretary of State unduly, but I would like to ask him when, as a matter of fact, we are to have these regulations, so that we may see exactly what the new commission intends doing. For instance, my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) asked a very pertinent question, whether any distribution was provided for as between the different provinces of those who were to enter the service, as had been provided in the United States when they began to do what we have undertaken-to give the preference to merit instead of to political patronage in Civil Service appointments. The minister says there is nothing provided in that regard. Is that absolutely so? It might happen that, for instance, Prince Edward Island would find within it so much talent that the 150 candidates necessary every year would come out of that province, and such
large provinces as Quebec and Ontario would get nothing. Surely that is a point which the Civil Service Commissioners have considered. Or are we to understand that there is to be no apportionments as between the different provinces, merit being equal? We all know what the former Civil Service examination amounted to. The Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) knows it very well. Heaps of men were piled up in the Civil Service without examination, but with the understanding that they would submit to examination later on. The Civil Service examination has become practically a dead letter. Since we are now adopting a step forward, and making a reform, we would like to make sure that it is really going to be carried out as intended.

If I may take it upon myself to answer :	I said there was no provision in the Act such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) speaks of. When the Act was going through parliament, the question was more or less discussed. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) was present, and I do not remember that he proposed to put such a provision in the Act.
No, certainly.

Then, I suppose he did not wish it to be put in. In his remarks, it seems to me, he is thinking more of patronage than of the good of the service. It seems to me that it does not matter much whether one province or another gets a little more patronage under the Civil Service Act, but it does matter a great deal that the best men should go into the service, and that is the object of reform, that is the object of competitive examination. I think the Act will carry out the intention we had in passing it.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I never had a more senseless answer to a reasonable question. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) seems to have patronage on the brain. I never spoke of enforcing any special enactment as to that. Nobody knows better than my hon. friend that there are a great many administrative measures that are not introduced into Acts and it seems to me it is perfectly proper for U3 at this stage, when we are voting the money necessary to have this Act put into execution, to ask if those who are going to carry it out have given that particular feature of the case some consideration. My hon. friend will not say that when the American people started out to accomplish a reform far greater than any that we have accomplished here, they did not display some wisdom in finding that they had to attribute a certain number of civil servants to each state. That is not put in the statute but it is a matter for consideration.
That is in the American statute.
I doubt it.
It is.

We are spending a large sum for the reform of the Civil Service and it is fair to ask if the consideration has been given to the attribution of the civil servants to the provinces of the Dominion in a certain proportion. For instance if a man from Quebec disappears from the Civil Service, will his successor be nominated from that province or will merit only govern? I am not advocating one side or the other but ask whether that point has been considered by the government or the commissioners. The answer of the Minister of Agriculture is that there is nothing in the law. If the committee think that is a satisfactory answer I do not. Can the minister give an approximate' date when we will have before the House the regulations that will govern the proceedings of the commission?

Since the hon. member made his inquiry I find that these regulations will be available within a week and I will have pleasure in presenting them to the House. I move that the item of $3,050, salary of the secretary, be reduced by $150, that the item of $2,100 for permanent examiners be struck out, and that the resolution be amended accordingly.
I would not consent to the adoption of the item unless assured by the minister that we shall have an opportunity of discussing the regulations.
Certainly.

There is a difference of opinion between the Minister of Agriculture and the Secretary of State. As I understand the Secretary of State, the examinations will take place at eighteen different places, and whoever holds the examination wi]l examine the papers, decide the number of marks of the candidates at these points, and on the number of marks sent in for each candidate, the commissioners will decide the special qualifications that he possesses. The Minister of Agriculture's statement is entirely the opposite. He states that the papers will be sealed up, sent in to Ottawa, and examined by the commissioners.

I think my hon. friend misanprehended me. I said that they would be sealed up and passed on by the commissioners, but as to whether they would be passed upon by the examiners at different places I did not know.
But the Secretary of State has a memorandum from the Civil Service Commission.
If he has, that is all right.
Then I understand that is to be final, and that what the Minister of Agriculture stated is not correct?
I am not going to set up my opinion against the Board of Civil Service Examiners.
Then that, I understand, is to be final?
Is there any provision for accepting the degree of a university or a teacher's certificate in lieu of an examination?
No.
Why not?
That was decided by parliament last session.

It is not too late to reform.
Resolution as amended agreed to.
Civil government-Post Office Department-Salaries, $488,944.

This item last year amounted to $376,831.25. This year it is $488,944. The explanation for this increase is as follows:-Increases in the salaries of certain employees raised from the minimum of their respective classes under the Civil Service Act of last year, $57,836; 18 additional employees made permanent under the provisions of the amendment to the Civil Serivce Act of last year, $57,836; 18 additional clerkships and 6 additional messengers, packers and sorters, $24,800; 20 increases of $100 each, $2,000; 442 increases of $50 each, $22,100 ; 3 increases of $46 each, $138; increases in provisional allowance, $650. I will take each item separately. First, let us take the Post Office Department, 1st division, subdivision A. There is the deputy head, Dr. Coulter, raised from $4,000 to $5,000. I need not give any explanation as to that as it was fixed by statute last year. The officers in Class A are all heads of branches of the department and have a large staff under them.
How does the superintendent of correspondence come to get a raise of $1,000 ?

He had a salary at $],-950 and besides he had an allowance of $600 as my private secretary making $2,250. He now loses the allowance of $600 and he becomes head of the correspondence branch so that the increase to Mr. Verret is only $350.
Is this a new office ?
Yes; it was recommended by Dr. Coulter.
The fact remains that you have actually increased his salary $950.
Has the minister made any new appointments in connection with this great boon of free rural mail delivery which he has conferred on the people?

In the province of Quebec Mr. Bolduc the chief inspector and in Ontario Mr. Ross, superintendent of post offices in Toronto, have been appointed heads of this service. In each province the inspector will be in charge of that branch of the service.
There have been no new appointments made in Ottawa in connection with that service ?
No.
And there are not likely to be any.
No.
