There would appear to be an increase of ten officials under this vote.

The business of the department has expanded considerably and we have had to appoint some new officials to cope with it. Mr. Moon has been promoted to be chief clerk; some fifteen years ago he was secretary to the then Postmaster General and I think he acted as secretary for Sir John Macdonald also. He is a very efficient officer and we thought he should be promoted. Mr. Martin an old and deserving official has also been appointed to a chief clerkship on the special recommendation of the deputy postmaster general.

The superintendent of correspondence received last year $1,950 and he apparently found time to act as private secretary to the minister for which he received $600 in addition. This year he has dropped that additional duty. In other words, while he does less work than before, his salary is increased by $350.

If the facts were as stated, I would say that my hon. friend had made a very good case. But I must explain that last year Mr. Verret, my private secretary, was a chief clerk as well. My hon. friend knows that the Post Office Department is naturally a department of letters. Every morning we receive heaps of letters from every section of the country, some addressed to the Postmaster General officially, and some in my name. The sorting and distribution of all these letters has to be done by a man who knows the business of the department. Of course, we have some French settlements in the maritime provinces, we have the province of Quebec, and we have many French people in the west, and if my hon. friend will consult
the Civil Service List, he will find that I have not one officer in the higher ranks of the department speaking and writing in French and capable of attending to and preparing answers to the correspondence in French. Mr. Verret, while acting as my private secretary, was assisted by four subsecretaries in attending to the correspondence. Now he will not have to do that work, but will be confined to the superintendence of correspondence in the department. I must have a first-class officer who is well versed in the two languages, and he is the only one out of twelve who is fully qualified for that work. He is a very competent and good officer, and I need him.
Will the minister explain to the House what his total salary was last year and what it is this year?
Last year is was $2,550; this year it is $2,900.

I would like to ask the Postmaster General if it is the policy of the department to maintain the sale of stamps as a monopoly. In the city of Toronto stamps could formerly be purchased from licensed persons all over the city. Now the sale is confined to the various branch post offices, where stamps can only be obtained during office hours.

The sale of stamps is a public utility, and the government alone can sell them. As a matter of fact, we have not reduced the number of licenses in the city of Toronto. Whenever the members apply for licenses in their respective constituencies, I am only too pleased to grant them, provided the licensees are a certain distance from each other. If my hon. friend will assign any of these licenses in his constituency, I shall be only too glad to comply with his request.

Has the minister any officer whose duty it is to examine into the literature that is coming into our country? Last session I called his attention to a number of undesirable publications coming into Canada, and I understood that some of them are coming in still in large numbers, as well as many others. The minister, by reducing the rate of postage to Great Britain has opened the door to a class of literature that is anything but of an elevating nature, while at the same time he has shut the door to the very best kind of literature coming from the United States. Our people are compelled to pay at least 50 cents a year for each monthly or weekly coming in, and at the same time he has placed on the weekly papers of Canada a ban that practically prevents them from having in the United States the circulation which they had for a number of years. I notice that the minister has made arrangements whereby these papers can go in to the United

States a little more conveniently than they could some time ago. I would like to ask him if he intends to continue the same arrangement that he had last year in regard to periodicals from the United States and in regard to Canadian weeKiies going into the United States.

As regards undesirable literature coming from England, I may say that during my recent trip to England I had an interview with the Postmaster General of Great Britain, Mr. Buxton, and I had with me the Hansard of last session, wherein my hon. friend referred to certain very undesirable periodicals coming into this country. Mr. Buxton answered by showing me a leaflet published by the Post Office Department of Great Britain, giving the names of the only periodicals which were authorized to come under the arrangement arrived at between the Canadian Post Office Department and the British Post Office Department. I know that the British Postmaster General is not willing to give to the undesirable papers the privilege which the legitimate periodicals have received through that arrangement, and I am sure, from the assurances that I have received from our officers and from numbers of the clergy of all denominations, that these undesirable periodicals have ceased to come through the mails. However, it is impossible to prevent them filtering in, for though they do not come by the Post Office Department, they may slip in through the Customs Department. I do not wish to shield myself behind my hon friend the Minister of Customs. We all know that as far as moral and sound literature is concerned, he is immune against any attacks that can be made upon him. I am sure he takes all the necessary precautions to protect this country against such undesirable literature. At any rate he has assured me that he has done so in the past. As regards the other question, the rates between the United States and Canada, I think we had better postpone to another occasion the very interesting discussion which no doubt we shall have on that matter. I may say however, that the weekly press have practically ceased sending protests. We have established at several points on the frontier, with the consent of the Washington authorities, means of sending the weeklies at the old rate, and since a few months, I have not received any protests.
Has my hon. friend received a petition from the post office inspectors to be placed in the inside service? And is he disposed to regard it favourably?

I have, but I would not like to speak for the government on this point. Last year, when my hon. colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, introduced the Mr. ARMSTRONG.
new Civil Service Act, he said it would first apply to the inside service at Ottawa, and that later on we would bring under the operation of the Act a number of officers. I would be quite willing to have the post office inspectors come under that Act, and have had applications to that effect, not only from the inspectors, but from the ordinary clerks and lower grades of the service as well. The outside service are quite willing to come under the operation of the Act, and also receive the bounty received by the inside service
Is the hon. minister considering the advisability of raising the rate of interest in the post office savings banks?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is- a question hardly proper to discuss under this item.
At all events we shall await the return of the Finance Minister.
I give the hon gentleman notice that I shall bring it up in another way.
When my hon. colleague (the Minister of Finance) returns, I presume that question would be discussed.

I would remind my hon. friend that the letter carriers of Montreal have petitioned his department for an increase in pay. I do not want to go into the merits of their demand just at present, but my hon. friend is aware that these men are getting very small pay for the work they do. Living in Montreal and having to pay the rent and taxes which prevail there and the schooling of their children, and the variety of expenses which only occur, or occur in a much larger degree in large cities like Toronto and Montreal compared with smaller places, their pay of $1.50 to $2 per day for the responsible work they have to do in,-all sorts of weather is very inadequate. They perform their duties faithfully and are well entitled to an increase, and I am sure that my hon. friend, who has made several improvements in the service in the city of Montreal, will consider favourably their petition.
I cannot say more at present than that the matter is under my very serious consideration just now.

Might I ask which official of the Post Office Department had to do with the extension of free delivery in the cities? We in New Westminster, encouraged by the statement of the Postmaster General a couple of years ago that he com-templated an extension of free delivery not only to the smaller cities, but to the tows as well, have been petitioning the department for an extension of that service

to New Westminister. In the meantime we have seen the service extended to other places with lower standards of population and revenue-for instance Three Rivers and St. Hvacinthe.
What is the population and what is the revenue of New Westminster ?
Our population is something over 12,000, and our revenue considerably over $20,000.

I am very glad my hon. friend has brought to my attention the case of New Westminister. I did not know it had a population of 12,000 and a revenue of over $20,000. If such be the case, I invite my hon. friend to my office, and he will be given letter carriage in that city. The rule we have adopted is that wherever there is a population of 12,000 and a revenue of at least $20,000, that city will be entitled to free delivery.

I have a statement from the mayor of New Westminster, and I believe it was sent to the department, of an official census, showing the population of New Westminster to be 12,198, and that the revenue is over $20,000 is established by the official reports.

If you have the population and the revenues and your city will number the streets, it will not take fifteen days before it gets letter carrier delivery.
Post Office Department-Contingencies (including $50 a year to pay W. Cooch for inspecting letter carriers' boots) $65,755.

There is an increase here of $14,000. It is made up of: Printing, $11,000; sundries, $3,200. The increase in the amount of printing is due to the increase of the business of the department. A part is the printing of the forms and pamphlet which I shall distribute in a few days to hon. members in explanation of, and for carrying on, the rural mail delivery service. Out of the item of sundries, we pay for newspapers, telegrams, telephones, washing towels, travelling expenses of officers on duty and various other items.
Does the Postmaster General intend to establish free mail delivery wherever it is petitioned for ?

Certainly-according to the principles of the Post Office Department. I will explain that in a few days. Of course, it will be on existing stage routes. It will be established as we receive requests,-we are not going to differentiate.
Will any particular number be required on the petition ?
Of course, we cannot give free rural mail delivery for one individual. But, generally speaking, where twenty farmers
And they must agree to take the boxes ?
Of course, the letters could not be received otherwise.

And for a box $3 is to be
paid?
Yes.
Any other expense ?
No. The box becomes the property of the person who pays for it.
Why does the minister call this ' free mail delivery '?
It is free.
Is this printing of which the minister speaks done by tender ?
Our printing is all done by the Government Printing Bureau, but, of course, we have to pay the Secretary_of State. In other things, we buy nothing except by tender.
The Postmaster General of course, is aware that the American Bank Note Company do business with his department to the amount of $60,000 or $70,000 a year.

That is a special contract which covers not only the printing of stamps but also the printing of the Dominion notes. That contract is with the Minister of Finance. It was made, I believe, in 1897, and has been renewed once or twice since then.
Arts, agriculture- and statistics-Statistical Year-book, $6,000.
We will have to have a lot of discussion on that. Why not take item 7, Department of Public Printing and Stationery?
We were discussing this Year-book before dinner, and we had better dispose of the item, I think.

We have the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) here, and it would be better to take this item of Public Printing and Stationery and adjourn at a reasonable hour, especially seeing this is private members dav. There are a few of our friends investigating the Year-book, and they are not prepared to discuss it tonight.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. George Taylor) to say that the gentlemen about him want further time to consider this and to look up the facts? If so, I would not prevent them. If they wish to study the Year-book, by all means let them do so. Let us take another item the vote for exhibitions.

That is worse; take something easy.

Arts, agriculture and statistics-Exhibitions $75,000.
Does this include the $50,000 given annually for the Dominion exhibition ?
No, this is for foreign exhibitions.
How many exhibitions are provided for in this vote ?
One-that at Seattle next summer.
Was there a grant to the exhibition in Scotland last year?
We spent some money upon our own exhibit at an exhibition in Edinburgh; we do not give any grants to foreign exhibitions.
Would the minister give the names of the officers who were at the Dublin and Edinburgh exhibitions?
I would like to have also the list of those who represented Canada at the Anglo-French exhibition, with the salaries or allowances given to each one.
For what exhibition is this amount intended next year ?
The Yukon-Alaska exhibition at Seattle.
Would the minister give the details of the estimate?

Mr. Hutchison, the chief commissioner, has gone to Seattle. He informed me before leaving that he expected the building would cost a little under $20,000 and that the present staff, with the exception of three or four, will be required, but I have not his definite report as to which should be continued and which left off.
What is the nature of the exhibition, is it international or state or a county fair?

It is intended to include the whole Pacific coast of America. The invitation to Canada to participate was accepted on very strong representations from British Columbia and the Yukon. Other countries bordering on the Pacific ocean are also invited to exhibit and I understand are accepting.

Does not the minister think that the allowance of $20 a day to Mr. Hutchison, who receives $3,000 salary, is rather liberal? During 275 days of the year Mr. Hutchison drew at the rate of $20 a day or $5,500, and then there appears to have been a term of abstinence or rigid economy, 90 days, during which he was allowed only $10 a day. What is the explanation of these two allowances?

The $20 a day is allowed Mr. Hutchison during the period when he is actually on the ground of an exhibition. Of course, while representing Canada at the exhibition he has to take his share with commissioners from other countries and give entertainments and receive the guests of Canada at these exhibitions. As for the days when he is allowed $10, that is during the time that he was abroad working on an exhibition, but not having to do this entertaining, because the exhibition was not running and there were no other commissioners there and no people coming who would expect to be entertained by the representative of Canada.

Has there ever been any system whereby instead of guaranteeing a per diem allowance, Bills were sent in as representing the cost of entertaining visitors or distinguished persons with whom the commissioner might find it advisable to come into contact. Is there any basis upon which this $20 per diem allowance is fixed?

Yes, years ago when Canada had exhibits at the Chicago Exhibition, and, later on, at the Paris Exhibition and some others, that was the system. It was found to be very unsatisfactory. There were all sorts of petty little details appearing which were made fun of and created debate in the House and in the country which was felt to be quite unnecessary and quite undignified. The feeling was that the system should be changed and in the case of a man like Mr. Hutchison, who is not known probably to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, but who is known well to the older members of this House, there is no suggestion of thought that he does not spend the money exactly in the way in which it is intended.

I would like to ask the minister what system is followed in dealing with the accounts of the exhibition commissioner, and how it happens that accounts for 1905 are only being dealt with in the volume of the Auditor General's Report now before us, three years after the expenditure has been incurred?

I cannot give an explanation off-hand, but I suppose there were some accounts held over for discussion, or something of that kind or perhans they did not send in proper vouchers and the accountant in the department refused to pass them.

I was prompted to ask that question by the minister's statement that we should take the fact that this money has been spent by Sir. Hutchison as a sufficient warrantv for us to pass this vote without further inquiry, but on looking over this volume of the Auditor General's Report, I see the following:
Win. Hutchison, commissioner, living allowance, Maroh 27 to December 31, 1905, 279 days at $20.
That is his living alowance for 1905. It appears in the Auditor General's Report three years later, and it is not a reasonable supposition that Mr. Hutchison went without the money during these three years.
Without the details of the accounts of 1907, I can only imagine that it was an open account which ran along and which eventually was settled by Mr. Hutchison?
How is that if he was paid $20 a day?

I need not say to my hon. friend that if he was over on the other side of the Atlantic he might not have drawn the full amount that was due to him, but that the matter was settled up finally and the accounts closed three years later.' I have no other explanation to give of it at present.
Mr., J. D. TAYLOR. There must be some further explanation than has been given to
the committee. This item on the face of it bears evidence of having been the subject of serious discussion in the department. But, to proceed, I read here:-
Less cost of banquet $670.05, paid in 1901-5.
I think there is something about this item which ought to be explained.

I have an explanation to give my hon. friend which has just been given to me. Mr. Hutchison gave a large bannuet to his fellow-commissioners at Liege, and it was such a large thing and so unusual that he thought the cost ought not to be taken out of his living allowance. He therefore sent in a special account for it. There was considerable correspondence with regard to it, but I refused to allow it to be paid except from his living allowance and eventually it was settled in that way, and he was required to pay the expenses of the banquet out of his usual $20 a day. Although paid in 1904-5 the correspondence did not occur until 1907, and therefore the account appears in the report of 1908.

This is exactly the same thing. Miss Barry made some charges and sent in bills for some things which we could not allow, but which she looked upon as being over and above her living allowance. There was a long correspondence, and the account was finally settled on the basis of the Auditor General's Report.
Who is Miss Barry?

Miss Barry is a lady who is well known in the city of Montreal. She is very much interested in the advancement of women's rights, she is a member of the Women's Council, and she was engaged to represent the ladies of Canada at one of these exhibitions.
Would the minister explain the method of exhibiting fruit at the Anglo-French exhibition?

The representation of the fruit districts of Canada was made as general as possible. We have to get the fruit which will show to the best advantage and keep the best. I was not present at the

Anglo-French exhibition, but I believe that most of it was shown in cold storage glass cases, and some was shown in the open. As soon as it began to deteriorate from contact with the air it was replaced by new fruit taken out of our cold storage which was not shown before it was taken out.
The fruit was gathered from all over the country and such fruit was shown chiefly as would keep the best. In the early days of the exhibition, starting in' May and lasting till November, that season's fruit could not be shown, and we had to get fruit of the season before. We had to keep that in cold storage, take it out and show it at the exhibition from time to time as the exhibition proceeded. For the first three or four months of the exhibition that had to be done, but later on we got the earlier fruit and placed it on exhibition.

I am afraid the minister did not quite apprehend the drift of my remarks. I understand the government took the ground that it was better to exhibit fruit as Canadian fruit and not as special exhibits under the names of various provinces.
Certainly.

Of course I understand it was desired to show fruit that was essentially Canadian, but this does! seem to me to be a mistake. I am informed that a person who proposed to emigrate from the old country to the province of British Columbia went to the exhibition desirous of seeing British Columbia fruit. When he got there it was impossible for _ the commissioner to point out where the British Columbia fruit was, except-and I say this with all deference to our friends from Nova Scotia-except that of course it made its presence known by its superior excellence. Even though special advertisement was not given to the different provinces, it was in my opinion a great mistake to so mix up the whole fruit exhibit that intending immigrants could not ascertain which fruit came from a particular province. I am told that one man decided to emigrate to Manitoba, thinking that certain very excellent fruit was the product of that province, although I do not think our friends from Manitoba will be likely to admit that the growing of fruit is their long suit. I repeat that in my opinion it was a great mistake that there was not a clear line of demarcation between the fruits from the various provinces.

We decided years ago that the exhibit by the Department of Agriculture should be a purely Canadian; exhibit, and that we should not divide it on provincial lines. The latter was done in the earlier days and it was not a success. I have repeated and strong compliments from our rivals at these exhibitions directed to Mr. FISHER.
the fact that we made the one national exhibit. Australasia has exhibited over and over again in competition with us and she has shown her exhibit divided according to her states, and other countries have done the! same. We have gone on the principle that the Canadian exhibit in one harmonious whole should represent the Dominion of Canada, and there is an almost unanimous opinion, if not quite unanimous, that this is the most effective and best way to represent our country. I sympathize with the view of my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell), but as a matter of fact while there may have been a collection of fruit shown as coming from Canada, yet individual exhibits bear the name of those from whom they have been procured with their post office addresses so that the province whence the fruit comes would be indicated in that way, Although I was not at the Anglo-French exhibit, I am pretty sure there were boxes of fruit and individual plates of fruit marked as coming from British Columbia. On the whole our exhibits have been national and not provincial, and that is one of the chief reasons why they have attracted a great deal more attention than the exhibits of other countries.

While I believe in the policy of not making any special advertisement of a particular province, yet I was distinctly informed that this man was told by one of the commissioners in charge that he would not and could not show him any special fruit grown in a particular province.
At page D-13 of the Auditor General's Report it appears that the pavilion cost us $39,643, and that it was disposed of for $1,460. Is not that a rather cheap sale?	*

I must frankly say that we find it very difficult to dispose of those buildings. We had to erect this particular building in accordance with the regulations of the London County Council, which required a very expensive structure, and -we either have to take the building down ourselves and dispose of the material or sell the building as it stands. We contract to take the building away and leave the land as it was before we commenced to build, and I have no doubt that Mr. Hutchison did the very best he could and he probably thought himself lucky to be able to get anything for the building.
I see in the Auditor General's Report that Mr. G. P. McHugh got salary and living allowance from May 8 to November 29. Might I ask if he is a son of Senator McHugh?

I think so, but I am not quite certain.
Mr. HUGHES-Is it the custom of the department to employ the sons of -liberal members of parliament and senators?
Any good men we can get.
And there were none but good men?
I hope not.

At page D-11 of the Auditor General's report there is a deduction on account of the payments made in 1905-6 to Mr. James Brodie, secretary of the exhibitions. Was Mr. Brodie also given a banquet that year?

No, but Mr. Brodie unfortunately was taking larger pay than he had been authorized to take and eventually I had to recall Mr. Brodie to settle up his accounts, after having tried for a long time ineffectually to get a statement of them. Mr. Brodie ceased to be an employee of the department afterwards.
In 1908-9 there is a payment of $84.75 to Mr. Brodie.
That was the final balance in closing the account and settling up the matter.
Are these exhibits sold by the government?
No, we use them from year to year when they are fit to be used, but when they are not fit for use of course we cannot sell them.

In view of the fact that the estimates in all other departments are being cut down, and also in view of the fact that Seattle is a very strong trade competitor with our Northwest, and also because adding to the welfare of its exhibition would be rather a detriment to Canada than a benefit, I wish to enter a protest against voting this large sum of money for that exhibition.

I think my hon. friend hardly realizes the amount of money that is spent in these large exhibitions. For instance, in the Franeo-British exhibition, Australia spent $600,000.	$70,000 is a very
small amount to spend on an international exhibition.
The hon. gentleman overlooks the fact that this is purely a local or state exhibition.
My hon. friend is altogether wrong, as he will find if he consults the representatives from British Columbia.

I think the hon. minister shqjild at least have given us the number of officials for whom this money is intended. He is asking for a large sum in bulk without giving details as to how he intends to spend the moncj.

There will be something under $20,000 for a building, something under $20,000 for the whole staff, $8,000 or
$10,000 for printing and literature for distribution, a heavy item for bringing the exhibits which were in London last summer all the way across the Atlantic and across the continent to Seattle, and a large item for packing and taking out the exhibits and setting them up.
How many officials do you expect to have ?
Eight or nine altogether.
The minister has omitted a very important item, the item of entertainment.
That is included in the $20 a day payment.

Will the minister explain how there was such a difference in the daily allowance of the different officials at the Dublin exhibition ? For instance, we find Mr. Turcotte receiving for 290 days $3 a day, while Mr. Quinn received for 228 days $8 a day.
Mr. Turcotte is one of the permanent men, with a salary besides the living allowance of $3 a day, while the $8 a day to Mr. Quinn, one of the temporary men, included both living allowance and salary.

The hon. minister stated a few moments ago, in reference to Mr. Brodie, that the $84.75 was a final settlement of the account. If he turns to page D-14, he will find the following: 'James Brodie, secretary, salary, 3 months to March 31, 1908, at $1,700 per year, $425.'
My hon. friend will notice that the salary is up to the 31st March, 1908, while the $84.75 was paid in 1908-9, just after that date, and was a final settlement.
Has the department dispensed with Mr. Brodie's services ?
Yes.
For what reason ?
Because Mr. Brodie had been drawing a larger sum for his living allowance than he was entitled to draw.

The hon. minister in replying to my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) gave particulars of a banquet of Mr. Hutchison which cost $670. But that was not the only banquet. There were two, as my hon. friend will see if he looks at page D-10. I find here in connection with this item at the Liege Exhibition pay to Wm. Hutchison ' less cost of banquet $670.05 paid in 1904-5 and $885.45 1905-6.'
I am informed that that is the same banquet and the only item of that kind.

The minister explained a few moments ago that there was a change in the system. Formerly when the government gave a banquet the details came in and were paid for at actual cost, but my hon. friend wanted to help Mr. Hutchison and so he gave him $20 per day living expenses, to be spent just as he liked. Being an advocate of temperance, the hon. gentleman didn't want any expenditure to appear for liquor so he gave this allowance of $20 a day, out of which Mr. Hutchison spent about $10, and, no doubt, put about $10 a day in his pocket. Here was an expenditure of the people's money which ought to go to the improvement of the farmers. Then there is Miss Barry, living allowance, 61 days at $5 a day besides transportation, Montreal to Liverpool and Havre to New York, $200, and sundry travelling expenses, $157.25. This is just throwing away the money of the country. Here we have $75,000 asked for ' to pay for an exhibition in Seattle, and no doubt we will have the minister coming back for another $300,000. There will be the same story as in the case of the pavilion erected in Dublin at a cost of $39,000 and which was sold for a few hundred. What earthly use is there in spending money in the United States on exhibitions? It is high time these foreign exhibitions should cease. It is money just thrown away for the benefit of a large staff of officials such as senator's sons at $5 a day and $6 a day living expenses without any benefit to the country.
What is shown at these exhibitions? I presume the minister shows himself at them occasionally?
I have not been at one for five years except at Dublin.

I thought he must have been at Dublin judging by the large expenditure there. I notice some details of expenditure for a page or two, but surely there were other items besides what are found in these pages. I see that the Massey Harris Company are down for a binder complete at $150 and a plough at $50 and so on. Are there no other agricultural implement manufacturers recognized as well? Further down you will find an item for cheese purchased from one firm and another item 'pay to J. C. Sutherland for writing preparing and proofreading a pamphlet " The Twentieth Century in Canada," $250, and to the King's Printer for 20,000 copies of that pamphlet $723.93.' Were there any other exhibits than those recorded on these pages ?

Yes, any number of them. A great many are exhibits sent to all the exhibitions such as mineral exhibits and exhibits of a permanent character. We have found the_ greatest difficulty in getting our Mr. FISHER.
agricultural implement makers and other manufacturers to furnish us with exhibits.
I don't see why you sent binders to Dublin.
Binders are used in Ireland.
Not very largely.

My hon. friend is entirely mistaken. Lots of people from Scotland and England went to Dublin as well as the Irish and our agricultural implement manufacturers do a very large business in the old country and Europe generally. We have to get these exhibits as best we can. Our manufacturers are so busy supplying the Canadian demand that they will not look to the outside.
Are not the exports of these implements increasing?
Yes, they are much larger than they were twelve years ago.
Does not an apple tree produce more fruit ten years after it was planted than the first year?
Yes, but until it is planted it does not produce anything.
In connection with the Seattle exhibition, what kind of display is specially mentioned?

We propose to make a general exhibit. We hope to get .a lot of fruit from British Columbia and trust our hon. friends from that province will aid us in that work. Also from Eastern Canada to show that other parts of Canada produce excellent fruit as well as British Columbia. We hope also to send mineral exhibits from British Columbia and Eastern Canada. One of the officers of the Geological Survey has been arranging to get a mineral exhibit from British Columbia and hopes he will be able to succeed. A large proportion of the expenditure of these exhibitions is in connection with the general display which makes the Canadian pavilion the most attractive on the ground, such as agricultural decorations, ropes of grain heads and such things as that. These attract people into the pavilion and once there they examine the other exhibits and learn what Canada is producing.
What happened to that binder ? I do not see any reported sale ?
I am told we still have it. It was shown in London last year.

Is it intended to have, at the Seattle exhibition, any pamphlet corresponding to ' The Twentieth Century in Canada ?' If so, under what auspices will it be prepared ? I ask this be-

cause in pamphlets issued under the auspices of the Department of Agriculture I have observed that there was a tendency to ignore British Columbia and to convey the impression that agriculture is confined to the portion of Canada east of the Rockies.
I can assure the minister that that is a mistake.

I agree that that would be a mistake, but I do not think that it is the case. The literature we distribute is mainly that prepared under the auspices of the Immigration Department, although we have had some prepared by ourselves.
Who was 'The Twentieth Century in Canada,' prepared by?
It was prepared under our auspices. It was a former pamphlet of our own which was brought down to date by Mr. J. C. Sutherland.
He received $250, and travelling expenses $24. Is he one of the officers of the department ?
No, he is a newspaper man who is well acquainted with the general resources of Canada.
Is the Department of Agriculture in the habit of sending copies of its pamphlets to members of parliament ?
Not those sent to exhibitions.
It would be a courteous thing to do.
It shall be done, if the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) wishes it.

I think the suggestion made by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) is a very good one. The information in most of the literature issued by the Immigration Department has shown a peculiar tendency to stop at the Rocky Mountains, as if there were no province west of that. And, as I have come across the gentleman employed by the Dominion government, it has seemed to me that their knowledge was limited to that part of the country east of the Rockies. Of course we desire to see the Northwest and all eastern Canada thoroughly advertised, but we believe that British Columbia also should come in for its proper share. I trust that the Minister of Agriculture will bring pressure to bear on the Department of Immigration to have British Columbia given its proper space.
